articles.title: Lovable SEO: Why Your Lovable Site Isn't on Google (and the Fix)
articles.excerpt: Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev. Lovable SEO problems usually come down to one thing: a Lovable project is a client-side rendered React app, so the HTML a search engine first receives is an a…
articles.body: Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev . Lovable SEO problems usually come down to one thing: a Lovable project is a client-side rendered React app, so the HTML a search engine first receives is an almost empty shell, and all your text, titles and links only appear after JavaScript runs. Google can render JavaScript, but it does so in a slower, separate step, and other crawlers may not do it at all. The reliable fix is to serve real HTML for every page you want ranked, which for most growing products means pre-rendering or moving the public pages to a framework like Next.js. This post explains why it happens, how to check your own site in five minutes, and which fix fits which situation. Why isn't my Lovable site showing up on Google? Lovable generates React projects built with Vite.

articles.excerpt: If you're a contractor, trade or building-supply company, the earliest public sign of a project is usually a development application or a building permit. A rezoning in Toronto, a new detached garage…
articles.body: If you're a contractor, trade or building-supply company, the earliest public sign of a project is usually a development application or a building permit. A rezoning in Toronto, a new detached garage permit in Calgary, a renovation permit in Montréal: each one is a project that will need people and materials, and each one is published by the city. The data is open. The problem is that every city publishes it differently: different portal software (CKAN, ArcGIS and others), different field names, different date meanings, French in Montréal. This post shows the general approach for turning that into one weekly list of leads, and the Python to run it. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Canada Development Applications Actor used below. It's a paid tool (prices in the Cost section).

articles.title: Track Amazon best-seller rank changes over time with Python
articles.excerpt: Amazon's Best Sellers lists are a public signal, updated through the day, of what is selling in each category. One snapshot tells you what is popular. A series of snapshots tells you what is changing:…
articles.body: Amazon's Best Sellers lists are a public signal, updated through the day, of what is selling in each category. One snapshot tells you what is popular. A series of snapshots tells you what is changing : which products are climbing, which just entered the top 100, which dropped out, and whose price moved before they did. Amazon doesn't keep that history for you. This post shows how to build it: take a daily snapshot, store it as a file, and diff any two snapshots in plain Python. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Amazon Best Sellers Actor used for the data step. It's a paid tool (prices in the Cost section). The snapshot-and-diff part works with data from any source. The general approach Pick lists, not searches.

articles.title: Why your first MCP server doesn't show any tools (and a starter that fixes it)
articles.excerpt: Why your first MCP server doesn't show any tools (and a starter that fixes it) I've built MCP servers for LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Medium and Kaggle. Most of what went wrong with them wasn't the API logic…
articles.body: Why your first MCP server doesn't show any tools (and a starter that fixes it) I've built MCP servers for LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Medium and Kaggle. Most of what went wrong with them wasn't the API logic. It was small plumbing mistakes that the usual starters don't protect you from. So I pulled the fixes into one small template: mcp-server-starter (TypeScript, MIT). Why most MCP starters break The common failures look like this: The server "connects" but the client shows no tools , or you get JSON parse errors. One bad tool call kills the whole server . A missing API key crashes on startup and leaves an unreadable stack trace in the client logs. An API key ends up printed in logs or committed in a .env . Nothing runs in CI, so a broken build only shows up when a user tries it. 1.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force launched an experimental Super Strypi rail-launched rocket carrying 13 tiny satellites, but it failed just after liftoff from Hawaii.
articles.body: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms.

articles.body: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.

articles.title: 'Trials and Tribble-ations' at 30: The classic 'Star Trek: Deep Space Nine' episode that brought Captains Kirk and Sisko face-to-face
articles.excerpt: How "Forrest Gump", pizza, and a massive supporting cast of furballs came together to make one of "Star Trek"'s finest hours.
articles.body: When "Star Trek" celebrated its 60th anniversary in September, it was a strangely muted affair. Sure, there were fan events, screenings, and even an attempt at a world record for the biggest simultaneous Vulcan salute in history , but the lack of a "Doctor Who"-style birthday episode felt like a glaring omission. It was like everyone had shown up for the party, but the organizers had forgotten to book the headline entertainment. Luckily, there were rather more fireworks for the show's 30th birthday, when both "Voyager" and "Deep Space Nine" marked the occasion in style. "Voyager" episode "Flashback" took Tuvok (Tim Russ) back to his days on the USS Excelsior bridge alongside Original Series vets Hikaru Sulu (George Takei) and Janice Rand (Grace Lee Whitney).

articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA's Swift space telescope crashed back to Earth today (Nov. 4), three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost the observatory to a higher orbit.
articles.body: NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road. Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit. The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.
